body.heading: Ask a room, start an argument
paragraphs: Hold up a drinking straw and ask: how many holes does this have? Some people say two — one at each end. Some say one — a single tunnel running through it. A few say zero, arguing a hole must be punched through something, and a straw was made this way.
This question became famous because intelligent people defend different answers with complete confidence. The disagreement is not really about the straw. It is about what the word 'hole' means.

body.heading: Openings or tunnels?
paragraphs: If a hole means an opening, the straw has two. If a hole means a passage through an object — the tunnel itself — the straw has one: the same tunnel you sip through, entered from either end. A mug handle, counted this second way, also has one hole, which is why mathematicians who study shapes, topologists, often answer 'one' for the straw too.

In topology, what matters is the tunnel, not the entrances. A straw's surface can be stretched and squashed in the imagination without tearing, and the count of tunnels survives every stretch. That is the deep idea hiding in the silly question: some properties of a shape do not depend on its size or squishiness at all.

body.heading: Why the argument is the point
paragraphs: Most everyday arguments are straw arguments: people using the same word for different things, each certain the other is wrong about the facts. The fix is boring and magical — define the word first, then count.

So settle it your way, but settle it explicitly: 'counting tunnels, one; counting openings, two'. You have not dodged the question. You have answered it twice, precisely — which is more than most arguments ever manage.

takeaway: The straw doesn't change — the definition does: two openings, one tunnel, and a reminder to define your terms before arguing.
